newsitem.title: USA: A year later, Simpson saga is morbid pastime.
newsitem.headline: A year later, Simpson saga is morbid pastime.

text.p: Tourists pose for snapshots at the murder scene. Books about the case top the bestseller list. And legal scholars hold seminars to debate its effects on the criminal justice system.
One year after the verdict, the O.J. Simpson murder saga has proved to be more than just a momentary national obsession -- it has become a kind of morbid American pastime.

While some people say they are losing interest in the sensational case, millions are still watching TV talk shows, buying the latest supermarket tabloids and surfing the Internet to keep up with every new detail.

In fact, it has become so all-pervasive that when one prospective juror in Simpson's civil trial claimed she knew almost nothing about the 1994 murders of the former football star's ex-wife and her friend, hardly anyone believed her.
"The O.J. case has become such a part of the culture that it's hard to imagine anyone being immune from it," said Stan Goldman, a law professor at Loyola University.
With its tawdry tales of money, fame and murder -- all served up in daily instalments on national television -- the Simpson drama had all the ingredients to attract a mass audience.

Today the case is not only a staple of pop culture, lining store shelves with more than 50 books and giving standup comedians an endless supply of joke material. But it has also made its way into intellectual circles.

Professors at Cornell University are assembling a Simpson research archive with a grant from the National Science Foundation. Law schools have made the case part of the curriculum, and legal scholars have held conferences to probe its impact on everything from juries to victims' rights.

The Simpson verdict sent shock waves through American society like no court decision in decades. The nation came to a momentary standstill last Oct. 3 when a mostly black jury, after only three hours of deliberations, cleared him of the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman.

The verdict split Americans along racial lines, with polls showing a majority of whites believing Simpson got away with murder while most blacks thought he was innocent. A year later, the racial divide remains -- making it all the more difficult to pick an impartial jury to decide the wrongful-death civil case brought by the victims' families.
Simpson is possibly the most famous American to ever face trial for murder, and many viewed his acquittal as a breakdown in the system, proof that the rich can buy their way out.

The trial, laced with tales of how Simpson abused and terrorised his ex-wife, also brought into dramatic focus the nationwide problem of domestic violence and helped bring about a series of legal reforms.

Mindful of the circus atmosphere that surrounded Simpson's criminal trial, judges nationwide have pulled the plug on courtroom cameras in high-profile cases. Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki has not only banned TV coverage of Simpson's civil trial but has also muzzled attorneys to keep them from battling each other with sound bites outside of court.

Under the relentless spotlight of the criminal case, a new breed of national celebrities was created. Attorneys signed multimillion-dollar book deals. Former Simpson houseguest Kato Kaelin became a radio talk-show host. One dismissed juror even posed nude for Playboy magazine.

Simpson prosecutor Christopher Darden condemns his behaviour and that of almost every participant in the criminal trial as "contemptible," but he sees nothing wrong with cashing in on his own involvement.

"I'm not ashamed or embarrassed by it," Darden said in a recent interview. He was paid a reported $1.3 million advance for his book "In Contempt," which has sold more than 800,000 copies, and now has a movie project in the works.
Tourists have turned the murder scene outside Nicole Brown's townhouse, Simpson's mansion and the victims' graves into major attractions -- part of a Hollywood tradition of ghoulish landmarks.
Simpson himself remains an object of intense public curiosity. Even a trip to the golf course can attract hecklers and end up leading the evening news.

Simpson has tried to repair his battered image, putting out a mail-order videotape to give his side of the story. Public relations experts say it may have backfired by showing him too willing to profit from his notoriety.
